transcript:
Meeting Header:
- Date/Time: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~42 minutes
- Attendees: Alicia Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Laura Adams (Vanguard CTO), Ravi Patel (Vanguard ML Eng), Sasha Kim (Vanguard Head of Platform)

[00:00] Alicia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alicia, AE on the account, and Marcus is our solutions engineer. Quick agenda, we'll do a live walk through of the model catalog, talk through benchmark numbers and how to pick open models for your workload, then cover deployment compatibility and security. Sound good?
[00:20] Laura: Yep that's perfect. We're really curious about how you recommend picking open models for our triage/clinical summarization workload.
[00:28] Marcus: Cool. I'll share my screen — give me one sec. (screen share noise) Alright so this is the model catalog page — you can filter by objective, size, quant profile, and we've got Redwood-verified benchmarks for latency and cost.
[00:45] Marcus: For example here we've got LLaMA2-13B quantized to int8, Mistral 7B, and Falcon-40B variants. Each model card shows throughput at different context sizes, 95th percentile latency for single-stream, and token/sec on our dedicated infra.
[01:12] Ravi: Quick Q — those latency numbers, are they on your hosted infra? What's the hardware baseline?
[01:18] Marcus: Good question. The default cards are measured on our hosted GPU pool: A100-ish equivalent for larger models, and Ada-ish for small ones — I know the labels aren't perfect in the UI. We include a hardware footnote, link to the full benchmark spreadsheet. For dedicated/private we run the same benchmarks on the customer's target HW if you give us specs.
[01:38] Sasha: When you say "same benchmarks", do you actually run the quantized kernels against our on-prem GPUs? How do you handle kernel compatibility for older drivers?
[01:45] Marcus: We do. For private/Dedicated POCs we do a candidate run — we build a compatibility matrix: driver versions, CUDA/cuDNN, kernel fallback. There's a small bit of variance when you hit older drivers, sometimes we fall back to a slower kernel path. We'll include that in the matrix we send.
[02:05] Laura: Our SLO is <150ms tail for short clinical prompts. Cost is important but latency is priority. Can you show which models hit that with prefix KV cache enabled?
[02:15] Marcus: Sure. If you look at the model detail page and toggle prefix caching, you can see the 95th percentile drops — for example Mistral 7B quant int8 with KV caching goes from 120ms median to about 90ms 95th on our hosted pool for a 512-token context.
[02:36] Alicia: Just to add, caching depends a lot on prompt repetition and sessionization. If your workflows are many one-off prompts, caching benefit is limited.
[02:45] Ravi: Makes sense. Also, how about hallucination / quality differences between open models? We care about clinical accuracy.
[02:52] Marcus: We publish a qualitative scorecard — the model catalog has an evals section with redwood curated benchmarks for summarization and factuality per model. For clinical tasks, we'd recommend a smaller set of in-domain evals; we'll map those to models and show regression risk.
[03:12] Laura: Can you explain the "model variant compatibility" matrix — you mentioned quant profiles. What's the tradeoff between int8 and q4_0/q4_k?
[03:20] Marcus: Yeah. Short version: int8 gives you better memory footprint but sometimes higher variance in outputs depending on the model architecture. q4_0/q4_k are 4-bit quant formats — q4_k tends to preserve more attention matrices for some transformer families. Our catalog shows recommended quant profile per model and the measured quality delta on a small eval set.
[03:40] Ravi: Are those quality deltas numeric? Like ROUGE / BLEU style?
[03:44] Marcus: We surface numeric deltas where possible (ROUGE, F1 for QA tasks), and a qualitative note for safety/factuality. The benchmark spreadsheet I'll send contains per-prompt deltas for the sample suite.
[03:58] Sasha: Networking question — for Private deployment we need VPC peering and customer-managed KMS. How do you integrate with HSMs?
[04:06] Alicia: We support KMS integrations and can do customer-managed keys; HSM integrations are part of the private package and we can discuss the specific vendor during the POC. We also provide audit logs and fine-grained RBAC in the private control plane.
[04:20] Laura: Great. Any compliance docs you can share? SOC2?
[04:23] Alicia: Yes, SOC2 and ISO are available, we'll attach those to the follow-up email.
[04:28] Marcus: Back to the catalog — here's the compatibility dropdown. It maps model -> recommended GPU families -> quant profile -> expected token/s and 95th latency. You can export the compatibility matrix as CSV.
[04:44] Laura: When you export, does it include notes about kernel fallbacks and driver requirements?
[04:48] Marcus: Yep, each row has a "notes" column where we mention fallback paths like "fallback to slower attention kernel on CUDA 11.2" — sometimes transcription in UI says "CUDA 11 two" but it's the versioning in the spreadsheet.
[05:03] Ravi: Ok can you demo selecting models for our use-case: clinical summarization with 512 token prompts, QPS around 8, and occasional batched runs overnight?
[05:12] Marcus: Sure. Filter by task -> summarization; set context to 512; set target latency 150ms 95th; show open models only. The shortlist shows Mistral-7B-q4_k, LLaMA-2-13B-int8, and a trimmed Falcon-40B-ctxt variant (but Falcon tends to be heavier on token cost).
[05:35] Alicia: Mistral tends to be a good balance: lower memory, good latency at 512 with q4_k. LLaMA2-13b int8 gives better accuracy on some of our medical summarization evals but at slightly higher latency.
[05:50] Ravi: For QPS 8 steady, is hosted OK or should we do Dedicated?
[05:55] Marcus: At QPS 8 with 512 context, hosted is feasible; cost-wise Dedicated reserved capacity often becomes attractive if you want predictable throughput and lower unit cost. If you need strict data residency or HSM, Private is the route. We can run a cost model after we know exact token counts.
[06:13] Laura: What's the expected start to POC timeline if we want to validate models on our infra?
[06:18] Alicia: Typical is 2-3 weeks to set up Dedicated/private POC: one week to get creds and infra specs, one week to run compatibility and benchmark, one week to iterate on prompts. We can compress if you have infra ready.
[06:30] Sasha: We have on-prem DGX-2 nodes with CUDA 11.4 and older drivers on some hosts. Will that be an issue?
[06:36] Marcus: We'll flag that in the compatibility matrix. For older drivers we may need to update or pin a fallback; sometimes perf is worse but functionally it works. We'll include exact driver notes.
[06:48] Ravi: Regarding the evals — can we upload our in-domain prompts and get a regression alert if future model changes degrade quality?
[06:54] Marcus: Yes, Redwood Optimize ties model rollouts to eval sets. You can upload prompt sets and expected outputs; we run continuous evals and alert on regressions. That ties into the rollout policy — automatic rollback if a canary underperforms.
[07:12] Laura: Good. On security again: will logs or transcripts ever leave our VPC in private mode?
[07:18] Alicia: In Private mode, logs optionally stay in your environment. We support configurations where audit logs are delivered to your S3 or Splunk; nothing leaves without your consent.
[07:28] Sasha: Any special networking ports we need to open for the private control plane?
[07:31] Marcus: Typical HTTPS ports and SSH for initial setup; exact list in the security playbook. We'll send that.
[07:38] Laura: Cool. Back to benchmarks — can you show the CSV export and the column headers?
[07:43] Marcus: Yep — columns: model_name, quant_profile, gpu_family, driver_min, token_s, latency_p50, latency_p95, cost_per_1k_tokens, eval_task, eval_metric, delta_vs_baseline, notes.
[08:00] Ravi: Nice. For cost modeling, how granular is the cost_per_1k_tokens? Can we get per-route breakdowns?
[08:06] Alicia: In the console we have token-level cost breakdown per route/model, and you can assign routes to teams. Redwood Optimize gives suggestions like batch-size increases or changed quant to hit cost/latency targets.
[08:18] Laura: What about streaming and function-calling interoperability with these open models?
[08:22] Marcus: Streaming is supported at the runtime layer; function/tool calling is higher-level — models that support structured output are flagged in the catalog. For example LLaMA-2 variants we tested with structured output via our output parser and function schema. Sometimes the structured quality is model-dependent.
[08:40] Ravi: Any gotchas around tokenization differences across models when you compare cost?
[08:44] Marcus: Yes — tokenization can change token counts significantly (e.g., GPT-like vs LLaMA tokenizers). The export includes a tokenization column and token counts are normalized to the model's tokenizer in the spreadsheet.
[08:58] Sasha: Are there examples of other healthcare customers who did a similar POC?
[09:02] Alicia: We have case studies — I'll send links. For confidentiality we anonymize specifics, but we can share high-level numbers.
[09:08] Laura: Great. Can you walk through a sample row in the compatibility CSV showing the fallback note?
[09:12] Marcus: Sure — here's one row: "LLaMA-2-13B, int8, A100, cuda11.7, 180 tok/s, p95 140ms, cost $0.08/1k, summarization, rougeL 0.62, delta -0.01, notes: fallback to slower attention kernel on cuda11.2 drivers".
[09:33] Ravi: That helps. For our nightly batched runs, would batching help cost without impacting latency for foreground traffic?
[09:39] Marcus: Yes — we recommend segregating batch workloads onto separate capacity pools or using burst capacity. Redwood's autoscaler can prioritize tail latency for front-end routes and allocate leftover GPU cycles to batch jobs.
[09:53] Laura: Any limits on how many quantized model variants you can host concurrently?
[09:58] Marcus: We can host many variants but memory footprint matters. On Dedicated you can pin specific variants to a GPU pool. On hosted, we manage cold/warm caches and may fallback to smaller variants under pressure.
[10:12] Alicia: Quick pause — any other specific questions we should cover?
[10:15] Ravi: One more — for metrics, do you provide token-level cost attribution by user or by API key?
[10:20] Marcus: Yes per-token attribution exists by API key; the console allows per-route breakdown and tag-based billing.
[10:28] Sasha: Ok I'm going to note that for our finance team.
[10:31] Alicia: Great; wrapping up demo section — we'll share the benchmark sheet, compatibility matrix export, SOC2 and private deployment playbook. Next step is POC scoping: Marcus can run a quick infra compatibility pass once Ravi shares sample prompts and HW specs.
[10:47] Marcus: I'll also include a recommended shortlist with expected p95 numbers per model and quant profile.
[10:52] Laura: Sounds good. Proposed timeline?
[10:55] Alicia: Send benchmark + cost model by 2026-03-05, infra compatibility by 2026-03-10, and schedule POC scoping call week of 2026-03-09.
[11:06] Ravi: Works for us.
[11:09] Sasha: Thanks, this was helpful.
[11:12] Alicia: Thanks all, we'll follow up with links and the spreadsheet.

Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional transcription errors — e.g., "KV cache" sometimes "KV cash", "q4_k" transcribed as "q four k" in places, and some proper nouns like model names (LLaMA vs Llama) are sometimes miscapitalized.

References/Links mentioned: https://redwood.ai/models, benchmark spreadsheet (to be sent), SOC2 and security playbook (to be sent).
